entry: Archaeological site of a pre-Columbian city in southwestern Illinois, directly across the [[Mississippi River]] from present-day [[St. Louis]]. The city existed from c. 1050 to c. 1350 and was the largest and most influential urban settlement of the Mississippian culture, which developed societies across much of the central and southeastern United States from around 1000. At its apex, around 1100, it covered about 6 square miles (16 km²) and had a population of between 15,000 and 20,000 people. Its original name is unknown; the mounds were later named after the Cahokia tribe, a historic Illiniwek people living there when French explorers arrived in the 17th century. The park covers 2,200 acres and contains about 80 manmade mounds, the largest pre-Columbian earthen construction in the Americas north of [[Mexico]]. It is one of 26 [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site|World Heritage Sites]] in the United States and a National Historic Landmark.

Chinese [[Eunuch|eunuch]] court official of the [[Han dynasty|Eastern Han dynasty]], traditionally credited with improving [[Paper|papermaking]].

In AD 105 he substantially improved the process by using tree bark, hemp waste, old rags and fishnets. The new paper quickly displaced [[Bamboo]] and wooden slips for writing, and Cai received wealth and fame throughout the empire. Earlier paper had existed since the 3rd century BC, so his contribution is usually described as an innovation rather than an invention. He served at the imperial court in [[Luoyang]] and was made a marquis in AD 114. After his ally, Empress Dowager Deng, died, he was ordered to the Ministry of Justice over his role in the death of Consort Song. Expecting a death sentence, he took his own life. He is revered in ancestor worship and deified as the god of papermaking, and he is the only early figure among China's Four Great Inventions whose name is known.

Crocodilian reptile of the subfamily Caimaninae, native to [[Central America]] and [[South America]]. Caimans inhabit [[Marsh|marshes]], [[Swamp|swamps]], lakes and [[Mangrove|mangrove]] rivers and are fairly nocturnal. Most species have an average maximum weight of 6 to 40 kg (13 to 88 lb), but the black caiman (*Melanosuchus niger*) can grow more than 4 m (13 ft) long and weigh more than 450 kg (990 lb), making it the largest caiman species. Caimans differ from their closest relatives, the [[Alligator|alligators]], in lacking a bony septum between the nostrils and in having longer, sharper teeth. Their diet largely consists of fish, and humans are their main predators because of hunting for meat and skin. Females build a large nest and lay between 10 and 50 eggs, which hatch within about six weeks.

Brothers, the first two sons of [[Adam and Eve]] in the [[Book of Genesis]]. Cain, the firstborn, was a farmer, and Abel was a shepherd. Both made [[Sacrifice|sacrifices]] to God, but God favored Abel's offering over Cain's. Cain killed Abel, and when God asked where his brother was, he replied, "Am I my brother's keeper?" God judged it murder and cursed Cain to a life of wandering, but gave him a mark to protect him. Cain settled in the land of Nod, where he built a city. Jewish, Muslim and Christian traditions regard Cain as the first murderer and liar and Abel as the first victim. The brothers have become enduring symbols of fratricide and sibling conflict in art, literature, theater, music and film.

American media personality and retired [[Decathlon|decathlete]]. Jenner won the men's decathlon at the 1976 Summer [[Olympic Games|Olympics]] in [[Montreal]]. Jenner later established a career in television, including the reality series *Keeping Up with the Kardashians*. Jenner publicly came out as transgender in April 2015 and is a transgender rights activist, although other LGBTQ+ activists have criticized Jenner's views on [[Transgender|transgender]] issues. Jenner ran as a [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] in the 2021 California gubernatorial recall election, finishing 13th with one percent of the vote.

Baked [[Dessert|dessert]] made by combining [[Flour|flour]] with a liquid, a fat or both, usually with a leavening agent. The word *cake* is of Viking origin, from Old Norse *kaka*. The oldest cakes were essentially sweetened breads. The most common ingredients include flour, sugar, eggs, fat such as butter or oil, and a leavening agent such as baking soda or [[Baking powder]]. Sponge cakes, leavened with beaten eggs, originated during the [[Renaissance]], possibly in [[Spain]]. Cakes became fashionable in the United States in the 1920s as women entered the labor force. During the [[Great Depression]], a surplus of [[Molasses]] led one company to patent a cake-bread mix, establishing the first line of boxed cake. When mix sales fell in the 1950s, marketers shifted the creative task to frosting and decorating.

Gourd vine (*Lagenaria siceraria*) of the family [[Cucurbitaceae]], native to tropical Africa and grown for its fruit. Also called bottle gourd, it is cultivated across the tropics. Young fruits are eaten as a [[Vegetable|vegetable]], while mature fruits are dried and used as ladles, bowls, beverage containers or musical instruments. It was one of the world's first cultivated plants grown not primarily for food but for use as containers. Calabash gourds can grow to great size; one grown in Kentucky in 2001 weighed 111.5 kg (246 lb). The name is sometimes confused with that of the unrelated calabash tree.

Region of southern [[Italy]], a peninsula between the [[Ionian Sea]] and the Tyrrhenian Sea. It has a population of 1,827,571 across 15,221.90 sq km, and Catanzaro is its capital. Greek colonies were founded on its coast from the 8th century BC, and the region was the heart of *Magna Graecia*. After the Gothic War it was a [[Byzantine Empire|Byzantine]] dominion for five centuries, and the Byzantines made it the main [[Silk|silk]] production area in Europe. Three historical ethnolinguistic minorities remain, speaking Calabrian Greek, Albanian and Occitan. It has three national parks, including Pollino, the largest in Italy.

Carbonate mineral and the most stable form of [[Calcium carbonate]] (CaCO₃). It is very common, particularly as a component of [[Limestone|limestone]], and defines hardness 3 on the [[Mohs scale]]. Calcite is usually white or colorless, though impurities can tint it gray, red, orange or other colors. Large calcite crystals are used in optical equipment. Its specific gravity is 2.71. The related mineral aragonite changes to calcite over days or less at temperatures above 300 °C.

Reactive [[Alkaline earth metal|alkaline earth metal]], chemical element of atomic number 20 (symbol Ca). Calcium is the fifth most abundant element in Earth's crust and the third most abundant metal, after [[Iron]] and [[Aluminium]]. Its name comes from the Latin *calx* ("lime"), obtained from heating [[Limestone]]. Its most common compound on Earth is [[Calcium carbonate]], found in limestone and the fossils of early sea life. [[Humphry Davy]] isolated pure calcium in 1808 by electrolysis of its oxide and named the element. The metal melts at 842 °C. Calcium compounds are used in cement, paper, soaps and food supplements, and small amounts of the metal serve as an alloy in [[Steelmaking|steelmaking]]. Calcium is the most abundant metal in the human body, where its ions play a vital role in signal transduction, [[Neurotransmitter|neurotransmitter]] release, muscle contraction and bone formation.

Common compound (CaCO₃) found in rocks as the minerals [[Calcite|calcite]] and aragonite. It occurs in [[Chalk|chalk]] and [[Limestone|limestone]], eggshells, shells, skeletons and [[Pearl|pearls]]. Limescale, produced when calcium ions in hard water react with carbonate ions, is also calcium carbonate. In the carbon cycle it sequesters large amounts of carbon in geological formations, and acidic water entering a deposit can form caves with stalactites and stalagmites. Heating calcium carbonate releases carbon dioxide and leaves [[Calcium oxide|calcium oxide]]. It is used as agricultural lime to correct soil chemistry, as a calcium supplement or antacid, and as a filler in [[Paper|paper]] and plastic. Excess intake can cause hypercalcemia and digestive problems.

Inorganic salt (CaCl₂), a white crystalline solid that is highly soluble in water. It is made by neutralizing [[Hydrochloric acid]] with [[Calcium hydroxide]]. Its hydrates are used mainly for de-icing and dust control, and solutions can prevent freezing at temperatures as low as −52 °C (−62 °F). On dirt roads, a concentrated solution keeps a liquid layer that suppresses dust, reducing the need for grading by as much as 50% and fill-in materials by as much as 80%. The anhydrous salt is hygroscopic and deliquescent, so it serves as a desiccant. In food, it is used as a firming agent in canned vegetables, such as tomatoes and cucumber pickles, and in firming soybean curds into [[Tofu]]. It was apparently discovered in the 15th century but was not studied properly until the 18th.

Inorganic compound, Ca(OH)₂, traditionally called slaked lime. It is produced when [[Calcium oxide|quicklime]] is mixed with water and forms a colorless crystal or white powder. Approximately 125 million tons are produced worldwide each year. Its saturated solution is called limewater, which turns milky when carbon dioxide is passed through it. Calcium hydroxide is used to prepare lime mortar, as a flocculant in water and [[Sewage treatment|sewage treatment]], and as a neutralizing agent in municipal wastewater treatment.

Quicklime, a white, caustic, alkaline solid of formula CaO. Also called burnt lime, it is made by heating [[Limestone|limestone]] or seashells above 825 °C in a lime kiln to drive off carbon dioxide. It is a key ingredient in [[Cement|cement]] and releases heat when it hydrates to [[Calcium hydroxide|calcium hydroxide]], a property used in self-heating food cans. When heated to 2,400 °C it emits an intense glow, called limelight, which was used in theatrical productions before electric lighting. Annual worldwide production is around 283 million tonnes, with China producing around 170 million.

Portable electronic device for performing calculations, from basic arithmetic to complex mathematics. The first solid-state electronic calculator was created in the early 1960s, and pocket-sized devices appeared in the 1970s after the introduction of the first "calculator on a chip." Integrated circuits reduced their size and cost, and by the end of that decade basic calculators were affordable and common in schools. Scientific calculators perform [[Trigonometry|trigonometric]] and statistical calculations, and graphing calculators plot functions. Calculator functions are now included in most [[Smartphone|smartphones]], making dedicated hardware calculators less common than they once were. In 1986 calculators represented an estimated 41% of the world's general-purpose hardware capacity to compute information; by 2007 this had fallen to less than 0.05%.

Field of [[Mathematical analysis|mathematical analysis]] that uses variations, or small changes in functions, to find the maxima and minima of functionals. Solutions are often found with the Euler–Lagrange equation. A classic problem is the shortest curve between two points on a surface, called a geodesic. Fermat's principle, that light follows the path of shortest optical length, is a related problem. The field began with [[Isaac Newton]]'s minimal resistance problem, solved in 1685 and published in his *Principia* in 1687, and with the brachistochrone problem posed by [[Johann Bernoulli]] in 1696. [[Leonhard Euler]] first elaborated the subject from 1733, and [[Joseph-Louis Lagrange]] contributed greatly to its theory. Euler renamed the subject the calculus of variations in 1756.

Large, cauldron-like volcanic depression formed when a [[Magma chamber|magma chamber]] empties and the ground above collapses into it. The depression may be dozens of kilometers across. Although often called a crater, a caldera is a type of [[Sinkhole|sinkhole]], formed by subsidence rather than explosion or impact. Caldera-forming collapses are rare, with nine known between 1911 and 2022; the most recent were at Kīlauea, Hawaii, in 2018 and Hunga Tonga–Hunga Haʻapai in 2022. The term comes from Spanish *caldera*, meaning cooking pot.

City (pop., 2021: 1,306,784) in southern [[Alberta]], Canada, the province's largest city. Calgary lies at the confluence of the Bow and Elbow rivers, where the Rocky Mountain foothills meet the Canadian Prairies. Its metropolitan population is 1,481,806, and the city lies 280 km (170 mi) south of the provincial capital, [[Edmonton]]. It was named after Calgary Castle on the Isle of Mull in [[Scotland]]. Its economy spans energy, financial services, technology and tourism, and it hosted the 1988 Winter Olympics, the first Canadian city to do so. The annual Calgary Stampede, a ten-day event since 1912, features [[Rodeo|rodeo]] competitions and parades.

City (pop., 2026: 2.3 million), capital of Valle del Cauca department, southwestern [[Colombia]]. Cali is the main urban and economic center of southern Colombia and spans 560.3 sq km. Its name derives from the Calima, local Amerindians. Spanish explorer Sebastián de Belalcázar founded the city on July 25, 1536, and moved it to its present location in 1537. Because Cali lay outside the [[Inca Empire]], Belalcázar claimed it as his own territory. The city hosted the 1971 Pan American Games and the 2013 edition of the World Games. It has one of Colombia's fastest-growing economies.

Most populous U.S. state, on the Pacific coast of the western United States. It is bordered by [[Oregon]] to the north, [[Nevada]] to the east, [[Arizona]] to the southeast and the Mexican state of [[Baja California]] to the south. With a population of over 39 million across 163,696 square miles (423,970 sq km), it is the third largest state by land area. Spanish colonization began in the 16th and 17th centuries, and the area became part of Mexico in 1821. After the U.S. conquest of California in the Mexican-American War, it was ceded to the United States in 1848, the year the gold rush began. It was admitted as the 31st state in 1850 as a free state. Its capital is Sacramento, and [[Los Angeles]] is its largest city. With an estimated 2025 gross state product of $4.296 trillion, its economy is the largest of any U.S. state. [[Silicon Valley]], in the San Francisco Bay Area, is the center of the global technology industry.

Synthetic [[Actinide|actinide]] element, symbol Cf, atomic number 98. First synthesized in 1950 at what was then the University of California Radiation Laboratory, it was named after the university and the U.S. state of [[California]]. Its most stable isotope, californium-251, has a [[Half-life|half-life]] of 898 years, while ²⁵²Cf, the most commonly used, has a half-life of about 2.645 years. Certain isotopes emit neutrons, so californium is used to help start up nuclear reactors and as a neutron source in materials studies. Users must account for radiological concerns, because the element bioaccumulates in skeletal tissue and can disrupt the formation of red blood cells.

[[Roman emperor]] (r. AD 37–41). Gaius Julius Caesar Augustus Germanicus, the son of the general Germanicus and Agrippina the Elder, was the third emperor of the [[Julio-Claudian dynasty]]. He succeeded [[Tiberius]] and was assassinated in a conspiracy of Praetorian officers, senators and courtiers. Most surviving sources were written by senators and nobles long after his reign, portraying him as cruel and extravagant, and some historians dismiss many of the allegations as exaggeration or mockery. He pursued public works, including the Aqua Claudia and Anio Novus aqueducts, and annexed Mauretania as a province.

Instrument for measuring the linear dimensions of an object or hole, such as its [[Length|length]], width, thickness, diameter or depth. Calipers may read out on a scale, a dial or a digital display, or may be simple compass-like tools with no scale, whose span is transferred to another measuring device. Types include inside calipers for internal size, outside calipers for external size, and divider calipers, which mark out locations in [[Metalworking|metalworking]]. The word derives from a corrupt form of *caliber*. The earliest known caliper, with a fixed and a movable jaw, was found in the Greek Giglio wreck dating to the 6th century BC. The modern vernier caliper was invented by Pierre Vernier, as an improvement on the nonius of Pedro Nunes. Calipers are used in [[Mechanical engineering|mechanical engineering]], [[Woodworking|woodworking]], [[Forestry|forestry]], science and [[Medicine|medicine]].

Islamic form of government under a caliph, a political-religious successor to the Prophet [[Muhammad]]. Three major medieval caliphates succeeded one another: the [[Rashidun Caliphate]] (632–661), the [[Umayyad Caliphate]] (661–750) and the [[Abbasid Caliphate]]. The [[Ottoman Empire|Ottoman]] rulers claimed caliphal authority from 1517 until the caliphate was formally abolished in 1924 as part of Turkey's secularization. Sunni Islam holds that a caliph should be elected, while Shia Muslims believe a caliph should be an imam chosen by God from the Ahl al-Bayt. In 2014 the [[Islamic State]], led by [[Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi]], declared a caliphate in Iraq and Syria; such claims have been widely rejected among Muslims.

Form of strength training that uses body weight as resistance for multi-joint movements, requiring little or no equipment. Also called bodyweight exercises. It can enhance strength, power, endurance, speed, flexibility, coordination and balance, using simple movements such as pushing, pulling, squatting and balancing. Common exercises include push-ups, pull-ups and sit-ups. The word comes from the Greek *kállos* ("beauty") and *sthénos* ("strength"). The practice was recorded in [[Ancient Greece]], including by the armies of [[Alexander the Great]] and the Spartans, and in ancient China, where [[Han dynasty]] physicians prescribed it for health.
